passage:
The milk cooperative's cash book in Rampur lay open on Kunal's desk, and the line he had written in June still looked wrong: an advance of forty thousand, to a supplier who did not exist.
He had meant it as a loan to himself, to be put back by Diwali. Every month he found a reason to wait.
In September the auditors sent their dates. Kunal could not sleep. He could add another line to cover the first, or stop.
Next morning he put twelve thousand, all he had, into the cooperative account, and took the cash book to Zubin-bhai, the secretary, who had hired him.
"I made a false entry in June," Kunal said. "This is what I've returned. I'll return the rest."
Zubin-bhai closed the door. "It's bad," he said. "But you came before the audit. We'll correct the record today and tell the board. And you should speak to a lawyer this week."

qa.q: How much did Kunal put back into the cooperative account?
qa.a: Kunal put twelve thousand, all he had, into the account.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling after the auditors sent their dates?
qa.a: Kunal was frightened and sleepless, torn between covering the first entry and stopping altogether.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference for Kunal?
qa.a: Stopping instead of adding a second false line, returning what he could and telling Zubin-bhai himself before the audit found it.

qa.q: How does Zubin-bhai respond to Kunal's admission?
qa.a: Zubin-bhai calls it bad but values that Kunal came before the audit, and arranges to correct the record, tell the board, and urges him to see a lawyer.

grounding: Kunal, who made one false entry, stops before the audit, corrects the record with a trusted senior, and is advised to seek legal help.

passage:
For two months, Aiko had added a few extra hours to the Morel client's timesheets at the small Lyon design studio where she worked. Her rent had gone up, and nobody checked hours line by line. She told herself it evened out, that she often worked late unpaid.
On a Thursday evening in November she opened the third month's sheet and stopped with her hand on the mouse. She thought about her name at the bottom of every sheet.
She deleted the extra hours. Then, before she could lose her nerve, she knocked on Leila's door. Leila was the senior partner who had hired her.
"I've overbilled the Morel project. About nine hours over two months. I've stopped, and I want to fix it."
Leila was quiet for a long moment. "Thank you for telling me yourself. We'll credit the client this week. There'll be consequences, but this is far easier than if they'd found it."

qa.q: How many hours had Aiko overbilled?
qa.a: Aiko had overbilled about nine hours over two months.

qa.q: What does Aiko's pause with her hand on the mouse suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Aiko felt a growing unease about her name on every sheet, and realised she did not want to carry on.

qa.q: What steps did Aiko take once she decided to stop?
qa.a: She deleted the extra hours, went straight to Leila before losing her nerve, stated exactly what she had done and offered to fix it.

qa.q: How does Leila react to Aiko coming forward?
qa.a: Leila thanks Aiko for telling Leila directly, plans to credit the client that week, and says there will be consequences but that coming forward early makes it far easier.

grounding: A junior designer who padded timesheets stops, corrects the record and tells a trusted senior partner before it is discovered.

passage:
In the hospital's HR office, Kunal waited outside Jasleen ma'am's door with a printout shaking slightly in his hand.
Two months ago he had marked himself for overtime on two evenings when he had actually left at six. Just two. His rent had gone up, and nobody checked. The second time had felt easier than the first, and that had frightened him awake at 3 am.
"Come in, Kunal."
He put the printout on her desk. "These two entries are false. I made them. I want to pay it back, and I wanted you to hear it from me."
Jasleen read it, then looked at him for a long time. "Thank you for coming yourself," she said. "There will be a written warning, and the amount will come out of next month's salary. If someone had found this in the audit, it would be a very different conversation."
Kunal walked back to his desk on weak legs and felt lighter than he had in eight weeks.

qa.q: How many false overtime entries did Kunal make?
qa.a: Just two.

qa.q: Why was Kunal frightened enough to wake at 3 am?
qa.a: Kunal felt frightened because the second false entry had felt easier than the first, a sign of where it could lead.

qa.q: What did Kunal do right in how he came forward?
qa.a: Kunal stopped after two entries, brought a printout, admitted it plainly to a trusted senior, and offered to pay it back before any audit.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see Kunal coming forward?
qa.a: Jasleen respects it, thanking Kunal, and says it would be a very different conversation if the audit had found it first.

grounding: Shows an employee stopping after two false entries, correcting the record with a senior, and facing a much smaller cost than discovery.

passage:
Subject: Something I need to correct
Dear Sonali,
I'm writing to you as head of compliance because I made a mistake and I want to fix it before it grows.
Last month, to get a shipment released on time, I changed the date on one quality certificate by three days. The goods were fine; the paperwork was late. I told myself it was just a formality. Last week my team lead asked me to "do the same trick" for another batch. That's when I realised this could become a habit, and not only mine.
I have not changed the second certificate. I've attached the original and the edited copy of the first one.
I understand there may be consequences, and I'm ready for them. I'd like to meet this week to understand what I should do, and whether I should also speak to our legal adviser.
Regards,
Anirban

qa.q: By how many days did Anirban change the date on the certificate?
qa.a: By three days.

qa.q: Why did the team lead's request worry Anirban?
qa.a: Anirban felt alarmed that the 'trick' could become a habit for Anirban and others, so it could no longer be called a formality.

qa.q: Which parts of Anirban's email make it a strong way to come forward?
qa.a: Refusing to change the second certificate, attaching both versions, accepting consequences, and asking to meet compliance and possibly the legal adviser.

qa.q: How might Sonali see an email like this compared with finding it in an audit?
qa.a: Sonali can deal with it early and in full while it is one certificate, instead of discovering a pattern later.

grounding: Shows an employee who took one wrong step stopping before the second, correcting the record and going to compliance and a legal adviser.

passage:
Divyansh, you asked why I seemed so calm last month. I'll tell you properly, since you're my oldest friend.
So. Sarita, the one who topped accounts in college, was "borrowing" from the office petty cash. Small amounts. For my sister's college fees, when Papa's salary was delayed. I kept a paper note in my purse: amounts, dates, all to be returned. I told myself that made it borrowing, not taking.
Then one night I added it up. It was bigger than I'd thought. And I noticed I'd stopped writing the dates.
Next morning I went straight to our senior partner, Mr Iyer, before I could talk myself out of it. I put the note on his desk and said, "This is what I took. I'll return all of it." My voice kept breaking.
He was angry, then quiet. He accepted a repayment plan and put a warning on my file. I kept my job.
If I'd waited for the audit in March, I wouldn't have.

qa.q: What did Sarita keep in the purse?
qa.a: A paper note: amounts, dates, all to be returned.

qa.q: Why was Sarita alarmed on the night of adding it up?
qa.a: Sarita felt alarmed that the total was bigger than expected and that the dates had stopped being written, so 'borrowing' was no longer true.

qa.q: Why did going to Mr Iyer early work out better?
qa.a: Coming forward before the March audit with the note and a repayment plan meant a warning and a kept job, instead of being found out.

qa.q: How did Mr Iyer react, and what might have been behind it?
qa.a: Mr Iyer was angry, then quiet, likely disappointed yet respecting that Sarita came forward and offered to repay.

grounding: Shows a young accountant stopping, admitting to a senior and repaying early, which cost far less than being found out at audit.

passage: I sit across from Hafsa in the accounts section, so I saw most of it, though I can only guess what was going on inside her. For about a week in October she was quieter than usual. She'd stare at one spreadsheet for ages, close it, open it again. Once I saw her wipe her eyes quickly at her desk. On the Friday she printed something, stood up, sat down, and stood up again. Then she walked straight into the cabin of Joseph sir, the finance director, and closed the door. She was in there almost an hour. Later the office heard, in bits, that she had moved some figures between quarters to hide a shortfall in her project, and had come to correct it herself before the audit. Joseph sir called it a serious mistake and a brave correction. She wasn't fired; she lost her bonus and must have a senior sign off her entries for a year. She looks tired. She also looks like she's sleeping again.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do on the Friday?
qa.a: She walked into the cabin of Joseph sir, the finance director, closed the door and stayed almost an hour.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been feeling during the quiet week?
qa.a: Hafsa seemed troubled and anxious, staring at the spreadsheet and wiping her eyes, perhaps torn about whether to come forward.

qa.q: Why was going to Joseph sir before the audit wise?
qa.a: Coming forward and correcting the record herself cost a bonus and a year of extra checks, far less than being found out later.

qa.q: How does the colleague telling the story see Hafsa now?
qa.a: The colleague sees Hafsa as tired but more at peace, noticing she looks like she's sleeping again.

grounding: Shows a person who took a wrong step, stopped, corrected the record and went to a senior before being found out, at a smaller cost.
